hook: How can a transform turn a differential equation into a problem of plain algebra?
about: An integral transform turns a function \(f\) into a new function by integrating it against a fixed kernel: \((Tf)(s)=\int K(s,t)f(t)\,dt\). The Laplace, Fourier, Mellin, Hankel, Hilbert and Radon transforms are the best known. The area studies which functions each transform accepts, how to invert it, and how it converts operations such as differentiation and convolution into simpler ones.

The guiding idea is to move a hard problem to a setting where it becomes easy, solve it there, and transform back. Differential equations become algebraic equations, and convolutions become products. Operational calculus makes this systematic by treating differentiation as an algebraic symbol. The subject also includes moment problems, which ask when a measure is determined by its moments. It supports differential equations, probability, signal processing and tomography.

example.title: Solving an equation with the Laplace transform
example.text: The Laplace transform \(F(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt\) sends \(f'\) to \(sF(s)-f(0)\). Apply it to \(y'+2y=0\) with \(y(0)=3\). The equation becomes \(sY-3+2Y=0\), so \(Y=\frac{3}{s+2}\). Since \(e^{-2t}\) has transform \(\frac{1}{s+2}\), the solution is \(y=3e^{-2t}\). The calculus has been replaced by solving one linear equation for \(Y\) and looking up a table of transforms.

objects.gloss: The fixed function of two variables against which the input is integrated.
The transform \(F(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt\), suited to initial value problems.
The transform \(\int_0^\infty x^{s-1}f(x)\,dx\), the Fourier transform on the multiplicative group of positive reals.
The collection of integrals of a function over all lines or hyperplanes.
A product of two functions that most classical transforms turn into ordinary multiplication.
A formula recovering a function from its transform.
The numbers \(\int x^n\,d\mu(x)\) attached to a measure \(\mu\).

theorems.name: Fourier inversion theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,dx\). If \(f\) and \(\hat f\) both belong to \(L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\), then \(f(x)=\int\hat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi\) for almost every \(x\).

theorems.name: Convolution theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f,g\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\), then \(f*g\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\) and the Fourier transform of \(f*g\) is the product \(\hat f\,\hat g\). The analogous statement holds for the Laplace transform and convolution on \([0,\infty)\).

theorems.name: Lerch's uniqueness theorem
theorems.statement: If two continuous functions on \([0,\infty)\) of at most exponential growth have Laplace transforms that agree for all sufficiently large real \(s\), then the functions are equal.

theorems.name: Radon inversion
theorems.statement: A smooth rapidly decreasing function on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), \(n\ge2\), is determined by its integrals over all hyperplanes, and it can be recovered from them by an explicit formula. Radon treated the plane and three-space.

theorems.name: Hausdorff moment theorem
theorems.statement: A real sequence \((m_n)_{n\ge0}\) has the form \(m_n=\int_0^1x^n\,d\mu(x)\) for a positive Borel measure \(\mu\) on \([0,1]\) if and only if \((-1)^k\Delta^km_n\ge0\) for all \(n,k\ge0\), where \(\Delta m_n=m_{n+1}-m_n\). The measure is then unique.

theorems.name: Paley-Wiener theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(A>0\). An entire function \(F\) has the form \(F(z)=\int_{-A}^{A}f(t)e^{itz}\,dt\) with \(f\in L^2(-A,A)\) if and only if \(F\) is square integrable on the real axis and \(|F(z)|\le Ce^{A|z|}\) for all complex \(z\).
